specPoints.text: understand why covalent compounds do not conduct electricity
understand why ionic compounds conduct electricity only when molten or in aqueous solution
know that anion and cation are terms used to refer to negative and positive ions respectively

primer.text: From Covalent Bonding and Ionic Bonding you know the two families of compounds and the particles inside them. This note asks one question of both: can anything charged actually move? The answer decides whether a compound conducts, and it also introduces the names anion and cation for the two charges of ion.

lessons.title: Conductivity of covalent & ionic compounds
lessons.opening: An electric current is a flow of charged particles, which usually means electrons but can also mean ions. Covalent compounds have no freely moving charged particles, so they act as insulators in solid, liquid and gaseous form. Ionic compounds hold fixed ions in the solid state, but once molten or dissolved the ions move and carry the current, so those two states conduct.
keyPoints: An electric current is a flow of charged particles, usually electrons but sometimes ions.
Covalent compounds do not conduct, since nothing charged is free to move through them and carry the current.
Covalent substances work as insulating materials whether solid, liquid or gas.
Ionic compounds conduct in the molten state or in solution, because their ions can then move and carry charge.
Solid ionic compounds do not conduct, because their ions are fixed in the lattice and cannot move.

low.restatement: Ask one question of any substance: is something charged and free to move? Covalent compounds answer no in every state, so they insulate. Ionic compounds answer no when solid but yes once melted or dissolved, because the ions are then free to travel and carry the current.
low.analogy: Think of two buildings: one has no staff at all, the other has plenty of staff who are locked in during the day and released at closing time; only the second building can ever get work moving.
low.examPointer: Match the state to the answer every time: covalent never conducts, ionic conducts only when molten or aqueous, and the moving particles are the ions.

medium.restatement: Conduction is a mobility test for charge. Covalent structures fail it in every state, which is why they find work as insulators in transformers, equipment and wiring. Ionic structures fail it as solids, where the lattice pins the ions, but pass it when molten or aqueous, because the freed ions migrate under the applied field and carry the current.
medium.analogy: Picture two warehouses: one is empty, the other is full of trolleys chained in place; only after the chains are cut, by melting or dissolving, can the trolleys roll and move goods.
medium.examPointer: Use the application examples when asked to explain insulating behaviour: sulfur hexafluoride gas around transformers, silicone oils in equipment, and plastic coating on household wiring.

check.stem: What is an electric current, in particle terms?

options.text: A flow of charged particles, usually electrons but sometimes ions
options.explanation: Both carriers exist in nature: electrons in wires and metals, ions in solutions and melts.

options.text: A flow of atoms through the substance
options.explanation: Whole atoms are not the mobile carriers; the charged particles are.

options.text: A flow of heat through the substance
options.explanation: Heat flow is thermal conduction, a different process from electrical conduction.

options.text: A flow of neutrons
options.explanation: Neutrons carry no charge and stay in the nucleus; they are never the current.

check.stem: Why can covalent compounds be used as electrical insulators in any state?

options.text: They have no freely moving charged particles in solid, liquid or gaseous form
options.explanation: Melting or dissolving a covalent compound never frees ions, so no state offers a charge carrier.

options.text: Their electrons are removed during bonding
options.explanation: Covalent bonding shares electrons rather than removing them; the electrons simply stay bound.

options.text: Their molecules are too large to move
options.explanation: Molecule size is irrelevant; the point is that nothing charged is free to move.

options.text: Insulation works only for gases
options.explanation: Covalent insulators work in every state, from solid plastics to insulating gases.

check.stem: Sulfur hexafluoride is a dense gas used to insulate electrical transformers. What property makes it suitable?

options.text: It is a covalent substance with no freely moving charged particles
options.explanation: The gas insulates precisely because its molecules offer no mobile charge to leak current.

options.text: It conducts electricity away from the transformer safely
options.explanation: An insulating surround must not conduct; draining charge is not its role.

options.text: It is ionic, and ions hold the charge still
options.explanation: It is covalent; ionic compounds conduct when molten or dissolved, which would be a hazard here.

options.text: Its density blocks electrons physically
options.explanation: Density is not the electrical reason; the absence of mobile charged particles is.

check.stem: Why does an ionic compound conduct when molten but not when solid?

options.text: Melting frees the ions from their fixed lattice positions, so they can move and carry charge
options.explanation: The ions are always charged; melting supplies the mobility that the solid state lacks.

options.text: Melting gives the ions their charge
options.explanation: The ions carry their charge in every state; only their freedom to move changes.

options.text: Melting releases electrons to carry the current
options.explanation: The mobile particles in a molten ionic compound are the ions themselves.

options.text: The solid state has no ions at all
options.explanation: The solid lattice is made entirely of ions; they are just fixed in place.

check.stem: A salt solution conducts, but the same salt as a solid does not. What carries the current in the solution?

options.text: The dissolved ions, moving through the solution towards the electrodes
options.explanation: Dissolving frees the ions, and their movement through the liquid is the current.

options.text: Electrons flowing through the water
options.explanation: Electrons travel in the wires and electrodes; within the solution the ions carry the current.

options.text: Water molecules carrying the charge
options.explanation: Water molecules are neutral; they are the medium, not the carriers.

options.text: Metal atoms dissolved from the electrodes
options.explanation: Dissolved ions move; electrode metal appears only where ions gain electrons at a cathode.

check.stem: Define an electric current in terms of particles.
check.modelAnswer: An electric current is a flow of charged particles, usually electrons but sometimes ions.

check.stem: State in which physical states covalent substances can serve as insulating materials.
check.modelAnswer: Covalent substances work as insulating materials whether solid, liquid or gas.

check.stem: Explain why nothing in a covalent compound can carry a current through it.
check.modelAnswer: Covalent compounds do not conduct, since nothing charged is free to move through them and carry the current — they have no mobile charged particles.

check.stem: A salt is tested as a solid and again as a solution; only the solution lights the bulb. Using the conduction rules of record, explain both results.
check.modelAnswer: Solid ionic compounds do not conduct, because their ions are fixed in the lattice and cannot move; in solution the ionic compound conducts, because its ions can then move and carry charge.

lessons.title: Cations and anions
lessons.opening: The two charges of ion carry two names: an anion is a negatively charged ion, and a cation is a positively charged ion. During electrolysis the electrodes pull the two apart, with cations moving to the negatively charged cathode and anions moving to the positively charged anode, while the electrons themselves travel from the anode towards the cathode in the outer circuit.
keyPoints: An anion is a negatively charged ion, such as Cl-, O2- or the sulfate ion.
A cation is a positively charged ion, such as K+, Mg2+ or H+.
During electrolysis, cations move towards the negatively charged electrode, the cathode.
Anions move towards the positively charged electrode, the anode.
The electrons flow from the anode towards the cathode through the external circuit.

low.restatement: Two names, two charges, two destinations: negative anions swim to the positive anode, positive cations swim to the negative cathode, and opposite charges are the whole steering mechanism. The electrons complete the loop by flowing the other way through the wires.
low.analogy: It is like a dance floor with two DJ booths: the cations (one name) always drift to one booth, the anions to the other, and nobody needs telling twice because opposite charges attract.
low.examPointer: Anchor the memory aid: cations pair with cathodes, anions with anodes, and both pairings are opposite-charge attractions.

medium.restatement: The vocabulary of record: anion names the negative ion and cation the positive ion. Under electrolysis the electrodes impose opposite potentials, so each ion migrates towards the electrode of opposite charge, cations to the cathode and anions to the anode, while electrons carry the return current from anode to cathode outside the electrolyte.
medium.analogy: Picture a sorting machine with two chutes of opposite polarity: every item is pulled to the chute that cancels its charge, and the conveyor belt carries the overflow around the back.
medium.examPointer: In a metal the moving charge is electrons; in a salt solution it is the ions moving to the electrodes while carrying the electrons; name the right carrier for each setting.

options.text: A negatively charged ion
options.explanation: Anion is the name of record for the negative ion, as in Cl- or O2-.

options.text: A positively charged ion
options.explanation: The positive ion is the cation; the two names must not swap.

options.text: A neutral atom
options.explanation: An anion is charged by definition; neutral particles carry neither name.

options.text: An electrode
options.explanation: Anions move towards electrodes but are not electrodes themselves.

check.stem: During electrolysis, to which electrode do cations migrate, and why?

options.text: To the cathode, because it is negatively charged and opposite charges attract
options.explanation: The positive cation is pulled to the negative cathode by electrostatic attraction.

options.text: To the anode, because like charges attract
options.explanation: Like charges repel; the cation heads for the opposite charge, the negative cathode.

options.text: Nowhere, cations stay still during electrolysis
options.explanation: Migration towards the electrodes is the whole basis of electrolysis.

options.text: To both electrodes equally
options.explanation: Each ion responds to the electrode of opposite charge only.

check.stem: Which list correctly pairs each ion with its name?

options.text: Cl- and O2- are anions; K+ and Mg2+ are cations
options.explanation: The negative ions carry the anion name and the positive ions the cation name.

options.text: Cl- and K+ are anions; O2- and Mg2+ are cations
options.explanation: K+ is positive and therefore a cation; the pairing has mixed the charges up.

options.text: All four are anions, since all are ions
options.explanation: The charge decides the name; positive ions are always cations.

options.text: All four are cations, since all are charged
options.explanation: The negative ions are anions; being charged alone does not make a cation.

check.stem: Where do the electrons flow during electrolysis, according to the note of record?

options.text: From the anode towards the cathode
options.explanation: The electrons complete the circuit by travelling from anode to cathode outside the electrolyte.

options.text: From the cathode towards the anode
options.explanation: The stated direction of electron flow is anode to cathode; reversing it misreads the circuit.

options.text: Through the solution between the ions
options.explanation: Inside the electrolyte the ions move; the electrons travel the external path.

options.text: Electrons do not move during electrolysis
options.explanation: Electron flow through the circuit is an essential part of the process.

check.stem: When a metal conducts, and when a salt solution conducts, which particles move in each case?

options.text: Electrons move through the metal; ions move through the solution
options.explanation: The exam hint draws exactly this contrast: electrons in the metal, ions in the solution carrying the electrons' work to the electrodes.

options.text: Ions move through both
options.explanation: A solid metal contains no mobile ions; its carriers are the delocalised electrons.

options.text: Electrons move through both
options.explanation: In the solution the mobile particles are ions; electrons travel only the external circuit.

options.text: Atoms move through both
options.explanation: Neither case involves whole atoms drifting; the carriers are electrons and ions.

check.stem: Define a cation and give the examples of cations named in the note.
check.modelAnswer: A cation is a positively charged ion, such as K+, Mg2+ or H+.

check.stem: State the path the electrons take through the external circuit during electrolysis.
check.modelAnswer: The electrons flow from the anode towards the cathode through the external circuit.

check.stem: Explain why cations travel to the cathode during electrolysis.
check.modelAnswer: During electrolysis, cations move towards the negatively charged electrode, the cathode; opposite charges attract, so the positive cations are drawn to the negative cathode.

check.stem: In an electrolysis cell, anions of a dye gather at one electrode. Name that electrode's charge and polarity, and state which species would gather at the other electrode.
check.modelAnswer: Anions move towards the positively charged electrode, the anode, so the dye anions gather there; the cations gather at the other electrode, the negative cathode.

glossary.definition: A negatively charged ion, attracted to the positively charged anode during electrolysis.
A positively charged ion, attracted to the negatively charged cathode during electrolysis.
The process in which an electric current splits a molten or dissolved compound, with ions migrating to the electrodes.
A conductor dipped into the electrolyte, at which ions gain or lose electrons; the anode is positive and the cathode negative.
A material that does not conduct electricity because it has no mobile charged particles.

workedExample.prompt: Molten potassium bromide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. a) Name the ions that move to each electrode, using the terms cation and anion. b) Explain why solid potassium bromide does not conduct but the molten compound does. c) Explain why a molten covalent liquid still does not conduct.
steps: a) Cations are positive ions, so the K+ cations migrate to the negatively charged cathode; anions are negative ions, so the Br- anions migrate to the positively charged anode.
b) In the solid the ions sit in fixed positions in the lattice, so no charged particle is free to move and carry a current; melting frees the ions, which then move and carry the charge.
c) A covalent compound has no freely moving charged particles in any state — no ions and no mobile electrons — so it cannot conduct even when molten.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) K+ cations to the cathode; Br- anions to the anode. b) Solid: ions fixed in the lattice; molten: ions free to move and carry charge. c) Covalent substances have no mobile charged particles at all.
